A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same RouteSAE research. Their text, equations, figures, table, and appendices support comparison, including material relocated between the main text and appendices.

before.justification: v1 Sections 4.2–4.7 report original reconstruction, interpretability, feature-extraction, and routing-weight results on Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct. Appendix C supplies additional extracted-feature examples.

after.justification: v3 retains original evaluations and adds random-routing comparisons, threshold sensitivity, human–GPT-4o comparisons, inference routing weights, and feature-steering results.

M1.justification: The sum-pooled inputs, linear softmax router, probability-scaled layer selection, shared TopK SAE, and reconstruction objective remain unchanged. Equations 1–14, including the appendix hard/soft routing formulations, are retained. The steering examples demonstrate feature manipulation without introducing a revised RouteSAE component.

E1.justification: OpenWebText2 training and evaluation coverage remains unchanged. v3 Section 3.6 adds a limited generation-steering task: manipulating Olympic-related and maximal-effort features in responses to two questions, beyond v1's reconstruction and feature-interpretation evaluations.

E2.justification: The ReLU, Gated, TopK, and Crosscoder baselines remain. v3 adds Random routing, described as assigning uniform layer weights, to the KL-divergence, feature-count, interpretation-score, and reconstruction comparisons. Crosscoder remains excluded from KL evaluation.

E3.justification: The principal training settings remain unchanged, including the 100-million/10-million-token allocation and 512-token context. Added evaluation designs include threshold sweeps over 10, 15, and 20; human–GPT-4o assessment of 100 RouteSAE features; original-versus-clamped generation with activation set to 20; and TopK activation profiles on Pythia-160m in Figure 1.

E4.justification: v3 substantially expands validation through a routing-control ablation, threshold sensitivity analysis (Figure 5), human assessment of automatic interpretation (Figure 7), inference-time routing analysis (Figure 9b), and steering case studies (Figure 10). These supplement v1's sparsity comparisons, training-time routing analysis, and extracted-feature examples.

E5.justification: Both versions average interpretation scores over 100 sampled features per SAE and retain the same stochasticity caveat. Neither introduces repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. The new human–GPT-4o disagreement histogram reports validation outcomes rather than uncertainty in benchmark estimates.

E6.justification: v3 reports substantial new results for activation profiles, thresholds, human agreement, inference routing, and steering. Random routing sometimes extracts more features than RouteSAE but scores lower on interpretation; higher thresholds yield fewer, more interpretable features. The abstract's 22.5% feature-count and 22.3% interpretation-score gains remain unchanged.

T1.justification: The SAE definitions, routing probabilities, selection rule, reconstruction objective, and hard/soft routing equations are unchanged. No formal assumptions, theorems, or proofs are added; the expanded routing discussion is conceptual.

C1.justification: The abstract and conclusion retain the same claims about efficient multi-layer feature extraction, interpretability, targeted intervention, and the headline improvements. The introduction's new contribution list restates existing contributions; additional experiments support capabilities already claimed in v1.

C2.justification: v1's explicit feature-steering limitation is removed, and v3 interprets its steering examples as evidence of controllable intervention. v3 also interprets training/inference routing distributions as contributions from both shallow and deep layers, and Appendix B newly qualifies soft routing as having shown no clear experimental benefits.

D1.justification: v3 clarifies that KL evaluation substitutes the activation at the highest-weight layer, specifies uniform weights for the Random control, and discloses the steering clamp value of 20. The implementation table, optimizer schedule, preprocessing information, and repository access remain substantively unchanged.

R1.justification: The cited-work coverage and positioning against single-layer SAEs and Crosscoder remain substantively unchanged. v1's related-work section is preserved in v3 Appendix A; reference formatting and shortened author lists do not constitute new research positioning.

P1.justification: The narrative is substantially reorganized: related work and reconstruction analysis move to appendices, limitations follow the conclusion, and routing analysis precedes the case study. The introduction gains a contribution summary, while several methodological and interpretive passages are condensed or rewritten.

P2.justification: The conceptual Figure 1 is replaced by an activation-profile plot; architecture diagrams and existing performance plots are redrawn. New threshold, human-comparison, steering, and inference-routing displays are added. Table 1 and reconstruction results move to the appendix, whose formerly full-width example boxes adopt a two-column layout.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens validation of the central mechanism and evaluation: the uniform-routing control tests the value of learned routing, while human comparison and threshold sensitivity address weaknesses in v1's automatic interpretability assessment. Steering examples also support a previously deferred capability. These gains outweigh limited steering coverage and the retained Figure 6 caption claiming maximal feature counts despite Random sometimes exceeding RouteSAE.
